But if seats remain unfilled after the 14-day selection period, “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” [1] The Service is a federal agency.
  • Because Labor-policy researcher Rachel Greszler warns that “there would likely be political pressure from presidential Administrations to hire individuals for arbitrator positions based on their political leanings.” [2]
  • So When the parties cannot fill the seats, federal choices decide who can impose their terms. Choosing arbitrators for their political views threatens workers’ access to decisions based on their circumstances and needs. Concern for just treatment gives [NAME] a reason to protect workers from that influence.
HR5408_UNC_oppose_06.response:
Response The argument’s step from the power to appoint panel members to political selection rests on one advocate’s prediction.

  • Because Each side normally chooses a panel member, and the third seat remains “one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties” [1]. The service fills “any members not selected” [1], so this power arises only when seats go unfilled.
  • Because The support for political selection is the statement that “there would likely be political pressure from presidential Administrations” [2]. That passage gives no evidence about how such appointments are made.
  • So The bill does give a federal agency those appointments. The further step, that those choices would turn on political views, is supported only by that prediction. This response does not show that such pressure would not occur.

The arbitrator code published by the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS), the U.S. mediation agency, lists honesty, integrity, impartiality and general competence as qualifications for arbitrators. It addresses voluntary arbitration and does not set rules for how an agency designates panel members. The sources reviewed document a 2025 executive order directing reductions at FMCS, which concerns staffing and not arbitrator selection. Sources: [22], [27].

The sources reviewed have no rules or record on how the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS) would designate panel members; the arbitrator code addresses voluntary arbitration.

HR5408_UNC_oppose_07.support:
Point 7 The bill puts resources for pay and shared protection at risk through required proceedings and new legal fights.

  • Because Lawyers King and MacDonald warn that compulsory arbitration requires “complex and cost-heavy hearings” [24]. Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe names another cost: “Courts will be asked to interpret the new statute and define the limits of the arbitrators’ authority.” [16]
  • Because King and MacDonald name a direct risk to workers’ income: “This approach will direct employer resources to litigation and potentially decrease the amount of wages and benefits an employer can provide to employees.” [24]
  • Because Imposing terms by law also gives opponents a basis to challenge union funding. King and MacDonald argue: “The government will be involved whenever an arbitral-created contract requires fair-share fees. All of those contracts will be open to attack in our courts.” [24] These are fees for representing workers who do not join the union.
  • Because Those fees support help for members and nonmembers. Labor-law scholar Ann Hodges explains that a fee clause “permits the union to charge a fee for representation to those who do not want to join the union and pay full union dues.” [17] Yet “the union must represent all the employees in the unit fairly and in good faith.” [17]
  • Because Workplace access faces a separate legal attack. King and MacDonald argue that “any time this bill imposed a contract with union access rights, it would take property and violate the Fifth Amendment.” [24] Their claim is that requiring employers to admit union representatives takes a property right without paying for it.
  • Because Fee lawsuits can use up resources even when they fail. Reviewing earlier cases involving public-sector unions, Hodges reports that they “impose substantial litigation costs on unions that could otherwise dedicate these resources to representing workers” [17].
  • So Required hearings and new legal fights can use up money for wages, benefits and representation. Challenges to funding and workplace access also put the tools of shared protection at risk. Protecting people with little individual power gives [NAME] a reason to preserve those resources and tools.
HR5408_UNC_oppose_07.response:
Response The legal rulings do not establish the blanket legal defects the lawyers’ letters claim.

  • Because Hodges’s evidence concerns lawsuits seeking refunds of fees charged to nonmembers for union representation. Those claims “primarily seek retroactive application of Janus” [17]. This means applying Janus, a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on fees for government workers, to fees already collected. That record concerns a different kind of lawsuit from challenges to contracts at private employers.
  • Because Government involvement alone does not make bargaining fees invalid. In the case Hanson, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld financial support for private railway bargaining and held that the requirement “does not violate either the First or the Fifth Amendments.” [28]
  • Because The Janus ruling distinguishes bargaining with government employers from private workplaces: “In the public sector, core issues such as wages, pensions, and benefits are important political issues, but that is generally not so in the private sector.” [29] The letters’ argument about government involvement does not resolve that difference.
  • Because The U.S. Supreme Court case Cedar Point does not say that every right for union representatives to enter a workplace takes property without payment. The Court separates access to closed property from “Limitations on how a business generally open to the public may treat individuals on the premises” [30]. The legal result depends on the access granted and the place involved.
  • So The fee and access rulings do not show the blanket legal defects the letters claim. This response does not answer the costs of hearings that do occur, or of lawsuits that use up resources even when they fail.

strength.html: The researchers Slinn and Hurd report that Ontario parties often settle before arbitration concludes, which can reduce time and cost; This bears on how large the cost is.

HR5408_UNC_oppose_08.support:
Point 8 The bill can hold back pay increases after a real deadlock, including in later contract talks.

  • Because Under existing law, “upon reaching a good-faith impasse, the NLRA entitles an employer to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer.” [18] This means putting that offer into effect without union agreement after talks reach a real deadlock. The NLRA is the main U.S. private-sector labor law.
  • Because The bill instead requires parties “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [1]. Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe explains: “This employer obligation to maintain all current terms and conditions of employment extends indefinitely beyond the point when the parties reach a good faith impasse to the date the parties reach agreement.” [16]
  • Because The maintenance rule “applies not just to first contracts, but rather to all employers and all contracts.” [16] The bill’s process for reaching a panel is limited to “an initial collective bargaining agreement following certification or recognition” [1].
  • So Sometimes an otherwise lawful final offer would improve pay without cutting other terms. In those cases, the bill stops the employer from giving those gains on its own after a deadlock. Later contract talks have no arbitration option under this bill. Closing that way to higher pay puts low-paid workers’ living standards and chances to get ahead at risk.

In a federal case, an employer proposed and a union accepted temporary pay increases during first-contract talks. In early 2014 the employer gave no raise. Employees testified that a supervisor said the raise was tied up in negotiations. The union filed an unfair labor practice complaint, and a settlement implemented the wage increase with back pay. Sources: [31].
HR5408_UNC_oppose_08.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

HR5408_UNC_oppose_09.support:
Point 9 The bill closes an existing way for workers to end union representation they do not want.

  • Because Existing law allows an employer to announce, before a contract ends, that it will withdraw recognition of the union (stop treating it as the workers’ representative) after the contract ends. The employer may do so “upon receiving objective evidence that the union has actually lost majority support.” [32]
  • Because Workers use this process. A June 2025 report describes a Sunoco driver named Fifer gathering majority support against the union: “Fifer opted to submit his petition to his employer, who withdrew recognition from the USW union in accordance with the Johnson Controls decision.” [33] USW is the name of the union, and Johnson Controls is the 2019 labor-board decision that allows this withdrawal.
  • Because The bill requires continued bargaining “absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [1]. Decertification means removing the union as the workers’ representative through a federal election.
  • So Clear majority opposition would no longer be enough for the employer to withdraw recognition; workers would have to wait for an election. That adds an obstacle to ending representation they no longer want. Just treatment includes respecting those workers’ wishes about who speaks for them.
HR5408_UNC_oppose_09.response:
Response Requiring that workers’ wishes be confirmed through a secret vote does not itself treat them unjustly.

  • Because The bill keeps “decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [1]. Workers keep the way to vote a union out.
  • Because The argument’s own legal account calls an election “the preferred method for determining employees’ representational preferences.” [32]
  • Because A signature is not always a worker’s final choice. Describing workers who signed conflicting petitions, labor lawyers explain that a secret ballot allows a final choice without others knowing it, “insulating them from retaliation from whichever side they fail to support.” [34]
  • So The election requirement checks the majority’s wishes through a private choice by workers, instead of leaving the employer to act on signatures. Just treatment includes protecting that choice for every worker. The argument shows that employer withdrawal can be quicker, but speed alone does not establish that confirming the majority’s wishes is unfair.

HR5408_UNT_support_01.support:
Point 1 The bill protects a continuing voice for workers whose employer opposes their choice to form a union.

  • Because Delay can weaken that voice. The bill states: “The employers can use those delays to sap labor organization resolve and secure more favorable terms for the employer.” [3] To sap resolve means to weaken a group’s determination.
  • Because Talks must start within ten days of a written request from a newly recognized or certified union, unless both sides agree to more time: “Not later than 10 days after receiving a written request for collective bargaining” [3]; “or within such further period as the parties agree upon” [3].
  • Because The bill keeps the employer’s duty to bargain in place until an election removes the workers’ representative: “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [3].
  • So These rules strengthen workers’ chance to have their chosen group heard despite management’s opposition. Hearing people whose choice one dislikes puts acceptance despite disagreement into practice.
  • Because In workplaces with people of different races, continued union work gives people shared tasks across racial lines: “Union workers engage in collective action around issues of contract bargaining and workplace grievances.” [4] The same source also names discussion with “explicitly anti-racist” [4] messages as part of unions’ approach.
  • Because Research that followed white workers over time supports a link to accepting Black people: “our panel analysis suggests that gaining union membership between 2010 and 2016 reduced racial resentment among white workers.” [4]
  • So Protecting continuing union relationships also supports a setting for cooperation across racial differences. This gives [NAME] a further reason to favor protecting that voice.

The racial-resentment study concerns white workers gaining union membership between 2010 and 2016, not first-contract rules. The authors say that contact without explicit anti-racism strategies may not reduce resentment, and also state that unions facilitate discussion including anti-racist messaging. Sources: [4].
HR5408_UNT_support_01.response:
Response The argument treats a stronger bargaining role as acceptance of different people.

  • Because Existing law already requires employers and representatives to “meet at reasonable times and confer in good faith with respect to wages, hours, and other terms and conditions of employment” [1].
  • Because The bill adds a starting deadline: “Not later than 10 days after receiving a written request for collective bargaining” [3], which can be extended by agreement: “or within such further period as the parties agree upon” [3]. The bill also extends the duty: “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [3].
  • So The added rules concern when talks start and how long the representative keeps its bargaining role. Giving that representative a stronger role in negotiating work terms does not by itself show greater acceptance or understanding of different people. The argument moves between these meanings of being heard without defending the link. This response does not answer the separate step about cooperation across racial lines.

HR5408_UNT_support_02.support:
Point 2 The bill gives opposing groups help in hearing each other and a shared way to settle disagreement.

  • Because The existing system already allows voluntary mediation (outside help with talks): “The FMCS provides completely free, completely voluntary contract mediation services to parties engaged in negotiations” [5]. FMCS is the U.S. agency that helps employers and unions settle disputes.
  • Because The role of FMCS fits the problem: “In first contract mediation, a neutral third party comes in to help facilitate the bargaining process between parties that do not have a mature bargaining relationship.” [5]
  • Because After ninety days of talks, or a longer period both sides accept, “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [3] The service must “promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement.” [3]
  • Because If no agreement follows within thirty days of the request, or an agreed extension, the dispute goes to a panel with “one member selected by the individual or labor organization, one member selected by the employer, and one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties.” [3] If selection fails, “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” [3]
  • Because The panel’s decision must weigh both sides’ needs: “the employer's financial status and prospects” [3]; “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” [3].
  • Because The panel’s decision provides shared rules even while disagreement remains: “such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [3]
  • So Either side gains a legal way to get help with a difficult conversation. If talks fail, each side has a place in choosing a panel that must consider their needs. [NAME] has a reason to favor this way of working with people despite disagreement.
HR5408_UNT_support_02.response:
Response The argument treats a way to settle a dispute as more mutual listening without showing the understanding it claims.

  • Because The next step applies when “the Service is not able to bring the parties to agreement by conciliation” [3]. Then “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute and such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [3]
  • So Choosing panel members and having economic needs weighed concern how work terms are decided. A panel can settle those terms while the groups remain unwilling to listen to or understand each other. Settlement alone therefore does not establish the mutual hearing and acceptance the argument gives it. This response does not answer the separate step that either side can now get mediation help with a difficult conversation.

strength.html: FMCS already offers voluntary mediation and a March 2026 review reports 58 mediators against the agency’s stated need of 80–100. These facts bear on how much added help occurs.

HR5408_UNT_support_03.support:
Point 3 A firmer process for first contracts helps workers get enforceable acceptance of different identities and beliefs.

  • Because First contracts already provide tools for this. Workers at Kickstarter, a company, voted to “ratify their first collective bargaining agreement with their employer.” [7] Its terms say employment decisions “are not based on any protected status.” [8] The listed traits include “religion, creed” [8] and “political affiliation” [8].
  • Because Contracts give workers a way to enforce such rules: “Through procedures that address contract violations, union contracts can be used to hold employers accountable and compel them to follow anti-discrimination policies.” [9]
  • Because Contract terms can also adapt work to people’s differences. At Santa Fe Opera, workers won rules requiring “costumes, wigs, hair coloring, shoes, and make-up that are appropriate for a range of skin tones.” [9]
  • So For workers seeking these terms, the bill stops a first-contract deadlock from blocking the whole contract. It strengthens their way to enforceable protection from mistreatment for who they are or what they believe, and to practical acceptance of differences. That serves [NAME]’s value of accepting people who are different.

The toolkit cited here describes selected negotiated results in professional workplaces. Kickstarter’s first contract was ratified without arbitration, its discussion forum has no power to decide or bargain, and its arbitrator cannot add to the agreement’s terms. The factors the bill gives the panel do not name these terms. Sources: [9], [8], [3].

A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration (outside decision-makers setting contract terms) rarely departs from the status quo (the existing situation) in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says first agreements decided by arbitration should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions (new kinds of contract terms). Neither review tests this bill. Sources: [10], [11].

A 2009 legal review reports: “Experienced arbitrators generally believe that interest arbitration rarely results in a departure from the status quo in terms of economic and noneconomic working conditions.” [SEP 8] Interest arbitration means outside decision-makers set contract terms, and the status quo is the existing situation. A review of Canadian practice reports “recognizing that arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions.” [SEP 9] Breakthrough or novel provisions are new kinds of contract terms. The first-contract study says “the quality of the first contract that a union achieves is a direct product of their power” [UNC 7]. These sources do not test this bill. They also do not address settlements reached because a panel is possible, or contract terms that put existing practice into an enforceable contract.
HR5408_UNT_support_03.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

HR5408_UNT_support_04.support:
Point 4 First contracts can create lasting opportunities to understand different people.

  • Because Contracts have created regular discussions across workplace groups: “Union professionals have used their contracts to establish groups made up of managers and union members that meet regularly to discuss and address diversity issues.” [9]
  • Because Kickstarter’s first contract gives a specific example: “To hold quarterly meetings during the work day with the participation of employees and management.” [8]
  • Because Those meetings openly welcome different views: “Any participant may propose issues to address and invite employees who have a particular expertise or viewpoint to a meeting.” [8] Participants agree to “maintain a respectful atmosphere at all times.” [8]
  • Because Contracts can also require repeated learning about bias. Actors’ Equity, a union for stage actors, won a rule that “theaters will provide mandatory anti-discrimination and harassment training on at least an annual basis.” [9]
  • So The bill provides a way through first-contract deadlock. This helps workers turn proposals for continuing discussion and learning into workplace rules. Supporting these opportunities gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill, because [NAME] values listening to and understanding people who are different.

The toolkit cited here describes selected negotiated results in professional workplaces. Kickstarter’s first contract was ratified without arbitration, its discussion forum has no power to decide or bargain, and its arbitrator cannot add to the agreement’s terms. The factors the bill gives the panel do not name these terms. Sources: [9], [8], [3].

A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration (outside decision-makers setting contract terms) rarely departs from the status quo (the existing situation) in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says first agreements decided by arbitration should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions (new kinds of contract terms). Neither review tests this bill. Sources: [10], [11].

A 2009 legal review reports: “Experienced arbitrators generally believe that interest arbitration rarely results in a departure from the status quo in terms of economic and noneconomic working conditions.” [SEP 8] Interest arbitration means outside decision-makers set contract terms, and the status quo is the existing situation. A review of Canadian practice reports “recognizing that arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions.” [SEP 9] Breakthrough or novel provisions are new kinds of contract terms. The first-contract study says “the quality of the first contract that a union achieves is a direct product of their power” [UNC 7]. These sources do not test this bill. They also do not address settlements reached because a panel is possible, or contract terms that put existing practice into an enforceable contract.
HR5408_UNT_support_04.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

HR5408_UNT_oppose_01.support:
Point 1 The bill skips contract votes that make negotiators answer to union members who disagree.

  • Because Contract votes give members a way to question and reject terms. UAW Local 600, an autoworkers’ union, explains that members have “a very powerful right to ask questions about any resulting tentative agreement and vote it up or down as you wish with your co-workers.” [12]
  • Because Rejection can send disputed issues back to bargaining: “If the tentative agreement is rejected, the union may demand that the employer resume bargaining to resolve the issue(s) causing member rejection” [12].
  • Because In cases sent to arbitration (a panel deciding the contract), the bill makes the panel’s decision binding without requiring a member approval vote: “such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” [3].
  • So Members can support a union and still oppose particular contract terms. Arbitration skips their existing way to refuse approval and press negotiators to answer their objections. [NAME]’s wish to listen to people who disagree gives a reason to keep that way open.
  • Note Choosing a panel member does not restore a vote on the resulting contract. The bill gives the union “one member selected by the individual or labor organization” [3]; the panel’s majority decides the terms.
  • Because In states that permit required bargaining fees, a contract can also make nonmembers pay for representation in order to keep their jobs. The U.S. Supreme Court describes agreements “requiring all employees in the bargaining unit to pay union dues as a condition of continued employment, whether or not the employees become union members.” [13]
  • Because This payment concerns bargaining representation. The Court limits required nonmember charges to “only those fees necessary to finance collective-bargaining activities” [13]. Federal law also protects state bans on agreements “prohibited by State or Territorial Law” [1].
  • So An imposed contract with a lawful fee clause also makes workers pay for a bargaining voice they reject. Respect for dissent gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added burden on workers who choose not to join the union.

The argument about fees applies only in states permitting such fee clauses and only if a panel’s award contains one. The sources reviewed do not show a panel would include one.
HR5408_UNT_oppose_01.response:
Response The argument does not connect skipping final approval, or requiring bargaining fees, to less listening to or acceptance of people who disagree.

  • Because The union example in the argument gathers members’ views before final approval: “Our union’s bargaining process starts with a concerted effort to get feedback from you and your fellow members.” [12]
  • Because In that example, members also elect their bargaining committee: “Your local union bylaws contain democratic voting procedures for you to elect a committee to bargain on behalf of you and your co-workers.” [12]
  • Because Federal law protects members’ right “to meet and assemble freely with other members; and to express any views, arguments, or opinions” [14]. The bill’s binding award leaves those protections in place.
  • Because The union must represent people who disagree fairly. The court decision in the argument describes its “statutory obligation to serve the interests of all members without hostility or discrimination toward any” [13].
  • So The final vote adds power to reject terms and press for changes. Accepting people who disagree does not mean accepting their preferred terms, so the argument needs to show less hearing or acceptance of them, beyond less control over the outcome. This response does not answer that losing the vote removes one way members press negotiators to answer objections.
  • Because The same decision describes representation “on behalf of all employees in the bargaining unit” [13] and limits required nonmember charges to “only those fees necessary to finance collective-bargaining activities” [13].
  • So A bargaining fee pays for representation that must serve people who disagree too; it does not require them to agree with the union. The argument names a financial burden without showing that it makes them less heard or accepted. A reason to reject required payment needs a further link to this value.

HR5408_UNT_oppose_02.support:
Point 2 The bill gives either side a way around reaching terms the other group can accept.

  • Because Existing law requires both sides to “meet at reasonable times and confer in good faith” [1], but “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [1].
  • Because The bill lets either side request mediation (outside help with talks) after 90 days of bargaining: “If after the expiration of the 90-day period beginning on the date on which bargaining is commenced, or such additional period as the parties may agree upon, the parties have failed to reach an agreement, either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [3]
  • Because After the “30-day period beginning on the date on which the request for mediation is made” [3], unresolved disputes must go to arbitration, where a panel decides: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [3]. The clock starts with the request, not with the first mediation meeting.
  • Because Mediation helps the parties find a solution they choose. The federal mediation agency describes this feature as “Parties retain control of resolution” [15].
  • Because Required arbitration creates a competing path. A 2008 legal analysis of an earlier first-contract arbitration proposal describes the danger that “the parties speak not to one another, but to the arbitrator.” [16]
  • So Failure to agree starts the bill’s process for imposed terms even after sincere, good-faith talks. A side expecting better terms from the panel gains a way to avoid further compromise with the other group.
  • So [NAME] values listening to people with different views. That gives a reason to keep the need for both groups to work through their differences and find terms each accepts.
  • Note Extra time requires agreement: “or such additional period as the parties may agree upon” [3]. One side’s willingness to keep seeking common ground cannot stop the other from seeking a binding award.
HR5408_UNT_oppose_02.response:
Response The argument does not establish that arbitration reduces efforts to understand the other side, and current law does not ensure terms both sides accept.

  • Because Existing law requires good-faith talks while stating that this duty “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [1].
  • Because After good-faith talks reach a real deadlock, an employer can put certain earlier proposals into effect without union agreement: “an employer does not violate the Act by making unilateral changes that are reasonably comprehended within his pre-impasse proposals” [17].
  • So Keeping current law does not preserve a requirement that workplace terms win both groups’ acceptance. Agreement on terms is also a different test from understanding the people proposing them.
  • Because The bill requires parties to “make every reasonable effort to conclude and sign a collective bargaining agreement” [3]. It requires the mediation service to “use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement” [3].
  • Because Research on Canadian first-contract arbitration (FCA) gives evidence against the predicted retreat from negotiation: “Despite this, FCA is not accessed frequently and it is even rarer for a first contract (in whole or in part) to be imposed. Together these results suggest that FCA encourages collective bargaining by creating an incentive for the parties to bargain in good faith and negotiate an agreement.” [18] In that passage, “this” means the finding that first-contract arbitration cuts first-agreement work stoppages by at least half. That research covers systems with a work-stoppage rule that this bill does not state.
  • So The bill’s deadlines do not excuse efforts to reach agreement. The first-contract evidence challenges the prediction that a binding last step weakens those efforts. One side’s refusal to extend talks after sincere bargaining does not itself show less willingness to understand the other group. The argument’s reason depends on that missing link, not simply on losing the power to insist on more time.

The Canadian first-contract study reports that arbitration is rarely accessed and rarely imposes a contract. It also notes that Canadian applications require any work stoppage in progress to stop, a rule not explicit in the U.S. proposal it discusses. Sources: [18].

HR5408_UNT_oppose_03.support:
Point 3 The bill risks letting people who do not understand local groups override their different ways of working.

  • Because Construction bargaining reflects differences between places and trades. The Associated General Contractors of America, a business group, describes “local multi-employer bargaining structures that reflect regional market conditions, craft practices, and established area agreements.” [19]
  • Because The association names the specific risk: “outside arbitration panels unfamiliar with local construction markets could impose contract terms that fail to reflect the industry or local labor standards.” [19]
  • Because The bill lets a panel majority settle the dispute. Changes to its two-year award require both parties’ consent: “unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [3]
  • So The bill removes the need for both sides to agree before decision-makers who may not know the local situation set binding terms. A local group whose practices are misunderstood cannot get a correction through its objection alone.
  • So Listening to different groups includes taking their local experience and working practices seriously. The risk of overriding that knowledge gives [NAME] a reason to oppose moving final control to the panel.
  • Note The panel must consider “the size and type of the employer's operations and business” [3]. That broad factor does not give the affected trade groups a right to reject terms that miss their local practices.

The panel includes one union-selected and one employer-selected member, and its decision must be based partly on the size and type of the employer’s operations. The arbitrator code published by the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS), the U.S. mediation agency, says an arbitrator lacking specialized knowledge must decline, withdraw or request technical help. It says an arbitrator should comply with a party’s request to visit a work area. The code addresses voluntary arbitration and is applied to the agency’s lists of arbitrators. A 2009 review says both parties produce evidence to the arbitrator. Sources: [20], [10], [3].
HR5408_UNT_oppose_03.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

strength.html: These warnings and responses cite no record of how arbitrated rules have fit particular workplaces. Sources: [20], [10], [3].

HR5408_UNT_oppose_04.support:
Point 4 The bill closes an existing way to act on workers’ rejection of a union that no longer has majority support.

  • Because Union representation also covers people who disagree. The U.S. Supreme Court explains that the union bargains “on behalf of all employees in the bargaining unit over wages, hours, and other terms and conditions of employment” [13].
  • Because When a contract ends, existing law allows an employer with timely, valid proof of lost majority support to withdraw recognition. This means to stop treating the union as the workers’ bargaining representative. The NLRB, the federal labor board, states that “an employer possessing such evidence may withdraw recognition when the contract expires” [21].
  • Because The bill instead continues the duty until an election removes the union: “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [3].
  • So Even rejection expressed independently and strong enough for that existing process would no longer end the bargaining duty. Workers would need an election removing the union before the employer could stop bargaining with it.
  • So Respecting people who disagree includes listening when workers reject a group’s claim to speak for them. Closing a lawful way to act on those changed wishes gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
HR5408_UNT_oppose_04.response:
Response The argument does not show why confirming workers’ rejection in an election gives their changed wishes less of a hearing.

  • Because The existing process gives the employer an option to stop recognizing the union: “an employer possessing such evidence may withdraw recognition when the contract expires” [21]. That is an employer’s power, not a vote workers can themselves use to remove the union.
  • Because The bill makes removal depend on “decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [3].
  • Because Section 9 of the labor law allows a petition “by an employee or group of employees” [22] challenging the union’s continued support. If the labor board finds a question about representation, it “shall direct an election by secret ballot and shall certify the results thereof.” [22]
  • Because The labor-board decision used in the argument calls a board-run secret vote “the preferred means of resolving questions concerning representation.” [21]
  • So Workers can take their changed wishes to the board without depending on the employer. An election tests the workforce’s current choice, including the views of workers who did not sign the petition. The argument does not connect losing the employer’s option to act without that vote to less listening to or acceptance of workers who reject the union.

HR5408_SEP_support_01.support:
Point 1 Faster first contracts bring enforceable workplace safety rules within reach sooner.

  • Because The study’s estimate combines different systems: “There is not enough variation across Canadian jurisdictions in the use of different types of FCA to permit the analysis to estimate the affect of each type of FCA on incidence.” [4]
  • Because H.R.5408 requires referral to a panel: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [2]. The bill has no express matching rule to stop strikes. A June 11, 2026 legal analysis names the gap: “The bill also raises questions about the lawfulness of strikes and lockouts during these first contract negotiations.” [10]
  • So The study’s explanation about bargaining incentives does not separate the panel’s effect from the rule stopping strikes. The argument has not shown that the reported reduction carries over to this bill’s different rules.
  • Because The arbitration process covers “establishing an initial collective bargaining agreement” [2]. Boeing’s 2024 dispute concerned an existing contract: “After ratification of a new contract in 2008, employees approved two contract extensions in 2011 and 2014.” [11]
  • So Boeing shows the harm of strikes, not an effect of the bill’s first-contract arbitration rule. This response does not answer the ordinary inference that a settlement process can reduce some first-contract stoppages, including in the hospital and military-support settings in the argument.

strength.html: The Canadian first-contract study reports no statistically significant effect of arbitration on the duration of first-agreement work stoppages, alongside its reported reduction in their incidence. Sources: [4].

HR5408_SES_support_02.support:
Point 2 A binding path to first contracts helps care workers get protections against infection.

  • Because A first contract turns organizing into practical protection. First-contract arbitration (a panel deciding the contract) gives workers a “guaranteed path to get the benefits of a union contract” [5].
  • Because Those protections include actual safeguards against infection. Longmont United nurses won “the first acute care private-sector contract for RNs in the state of Colorado.” [12] That contract included “Health and safety provisions to ensure nurses get the highest level of personal protective equipment when caring for patients with infectious diseases.” [12]
  • Because Protective equipment is part of infection prevention. Guidance from the CDC, the U.S. public health agency, lists “use of gloves, gown, mask, eye protection, or face shield, depending on the anticipated exposure” [13].
  • So Binding settlement gives newly organized care workers a way to get enforceable protections that an employer cannot block just by refusing to sign any contract. Strengthening this way to protect care workers and patients helps the United States defend people against disease outbreaks.

Longmont United’s first contract was reached through bargaining under existing law. The bill’s five panel factors do not name infection safeguards. Sources: [12], [2].

A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration (outside decision-makers setting contract terms) rarely departs from the status quo (the existing situation) in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says first agreements decided by arbitration should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions (new kinds of contract terms). Neither review tests this bill. Sources: [14], [15].

The sources reviewed show protective-equipment terms at one hospital and federal infection guidance, but not how such contract terms change national outbreak capacity; the argument states this step without a source.

HR5408_SES_support_03.support:
Point 3 Protecting and improving pay and benefits helps the country withstand economic setbacks.

  • Because The bill makes a contract’s gains attainable and requires the panel to consider “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” [2].
  • Because The U.S. Treasury estimates a pay gain from union membership: “Unions raise the wages of their members by 10 to 15 percent.” [16] Treasury also finds better benefits and work rules: “These workplace improvements contribute substantially to middle-class financial stability and worker well-being.” [16]
  • Because Treasury links unions’ broader economic benefit to “reducing overall inequality.” [16]
  • Because The bill also protects existing pay during bargaining. It adds a duty “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [2]. This closes a way of imposing cuts: existing law gives an employer a “right to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer when the parties reach a good faith impasse.” [17] An impasse is a real deadlock in talks.
  • Because Financial strength has a national effect. Treasury explains that reducing inequality strengthens households, “making these Americans less sensitive to negative income shocks and thus lessening economic volatility.” [18] Negative income shocks are sudden losses of income, and volatility means large swings.
  • So Making gains from first contracts attainable and protecting pay during talks helps households withstand lost income. That strengthens the wider economy against swings caused by households’ financial problems, which supports U.S. stability.
HR5408_SES_support_03.response:
Response The income gain in the argument depends on a general union pay estimate that differs from evidence on new unionization.

  • Because Treasury’s estimate concerns union membership: “Unions raise the wages of their members by 10 to 15 percent.” [16] The bill’s first-contract process starts “following certification or recognition of an individual or labor organization as a representative” [2]. The pay gap between union and non-union workers does not measure gains for workers forming a new union.
  • Because Gains from forming a new union differ from the general union pay gap. A study covering 1984–2001 compared workplaces where unions barely won or lost elections. Its wage results, from manufacturing, were different from the general pay gap: “estimates for wages are close to zero.” [19] This is evidence that the measures differ, not an estimate of this bill’s effect.
  • So The general union pay estimate does not establish the income gain from new first contracts on which part of the stability claim rests. This response does not answer the separate step on protecting current pay during talks.

HR5408_SES_support_04.support:
Point 4 Settled terms give businesses a firmer basis for steady operations and investment.

  • Because The bill’s settlement is “binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” [2]. That gives businesses a known basis for planning labor costs.
  • Because The bill’s sponsors explain the planning benefit of lasting terms: “Companies also benefit from the multi-year contracts unions negotiate, which makes budgeting more predictable and long-term financial planning easier to manage.” [20]
  • Because The panel must base its decision on the business’s circumstances, including “the employer's financial status and prospects” [2].
  • So The bill brings a similar planning benefit through settled, lasting terms. More predictable labor costs help companies plan staffing, spending and investment, which supports steadier economic activity across the United States.
HR5408_SES_support_04.response:
Response The argument has not shown that moving labor-cost decisions to a panel makes those costs more predictable than under existing law.

  • Because At a real deadlock in talks, existing law gives the employer the “right to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer when the parties reach a good faith impasse.” [17] The employer can choose the costs of the terms it puts into effect.
  • Because The bill removes that option by requiring employers “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [2]. A panel then chooses unresolved first-contract terms. The panel’s duty to weigh “the employer's financial status and prospects” [2] does not tell the business what costs it will impose.
  • Because The ruling is “binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” [2], but the arbitrators “have no set time to issue their award.” [21] Those two years describe how long the ruling lasts, not when its costs become known.
  • So The argument counts how long settled terms last without comparing the uncertainty of a panel’s choice and timing with the employer’s existing control over terms it puts into effect. The argument has not established more predictable labor costs, so its step to steadier investment and national economic activity lacks support.

HR5408_SES_oppose_01.support:
Point 1 The bill adds required work to an agency that protects essential services and already limits the cases it takes.

  • Because The Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS) is the U.S. agency that helps employers and unions settle disputes. Requiring first-contract mediation when either side asks adds demand for its help. Former NLRB chair Lauren McFerran, who led the federal labor board, wrote in March 2025 about the proposal: “This mandatory requirement would presumably significantly increase the demand for the FMCS’s services, as opposed to the current, voluntary system.” [5]
  • Because FMCS would also have to fill arbitration panel seats when the two sides do not choose members: “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” [2]
  • Because The agency’s April 2026 budget reports limits on the groups of workers it serves: “FMCS limited its involvement to facilities that provide health care services with bargaining units of 250 or more members, and to bargaining units of 1,000 members or more for all other industries in which it has jurisdiction.” [23]
  • Because The bill provides no funding for more staff. The National Restaurant Association, a business group, warns: “The FLCA also assumes a significant expansion in federal mediation capacity that has not been funded.” [24]
  • Because FMCS describes its role: “Our mediators work tirelessly to minimize and prevent disruptions affecting utilities, health care, public safety and security.” [25]

HR5408_SES_oppose_01.response:
Response The argument does not show that added first-contract demand would take resources from urgent disputes rather than from other work.

  • Because Existing FMCS policy offers mediation in disputes “which imperil or threaten to imperil the national health or safety.” [26] Health-care mediation also carries an existing duty: “the Service shall promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to bring them to agreement.” [22] The bill does not remove that policy or the health-care duty.
  • Because The added panel appointments depend on disputes staying unsettled. Referral follows only when “the Service is not able to bring the parties to agreement by conciliation” [2]. In Canadian first-contract arbitration, the researcher Johnson finds that “the threat of having a first agreement imposed creates an incentive for the parties to reach agreement on their own.” [4] Those Canadian systems also had a work-stoppage rule that this bill does not state.
  • So The sources in the argument describe more demand and service limits, but not how the agency would divide staff among disputes. Existing priorities make taking staff from urgent disputes a separate step that needs support. This response does not deny that added cases would stretch a limited staff.

strength.html: FMCS already mediates initial contract negotiations, so the added burden is the extra work beyond this; this bears on how much strain there is.

HR5408_SES_oppose_02.response:
Response The argument does not support its claimed added risk of awards that a defense supplier cannot afford.

  • Because The bill requires the decision to rest on “the employer's financial status and prospects” [2] and “the wages and benefits other employers in the same business provide their employees” [2]. The panel must use the employer’s finances and pay at similar businesses when setting terms.
  • Because A 2009 review of arbitration that sets contract terms reports: “Experienced arbitrators generally believe that interest arbitration rarely results in a departure from the status quo in terms of economic and noneconomic working conditions.” [14] The status quo is the existing situation. This account of arbitration practice challenges the unsupported forecast of unaffordable awards.

The argument shows that defense suppliers matter, but not why this process for setting terms would make them more likely to close. Losing a right to reject terms does not establish that missing step. This response does not show that an unaffordable award could never occur.

HR5408_C01.support: The bill states the first step: “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [UNN 3] It states the next step: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [UNN 3]. The panel has “one member selected by the individual or labor organization, one member selected by the employer, and one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties.” [UNC 1]

HR5408_C02.support: The factors include “the employer's financial status and prospects” [UNN 3] and “the wages and benefits other employers in the same business provide their employees.” [UNN 3]

HR5408_C03.support: The bill’s words are in the verified provision above. Section 9 allows a petition “by an employee or group of employees” [UNT 22], followed by “an election by secret ballot” [UNT 22] when the labor board finds a question about representation.

HR5408_C04.support: The bill adds a duty “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [UNC 1]. Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe explains: “This employer obligation to maintain all current terms and conditions of employment extends indefinitely beyond the point when the parties reach a good faith impasse to the date the parties reach agreement.” [UNC 16] He adds that it “applies not just to first contracts, but rather to all employers and all contracts.” [UNC 16]

HR5408_C05.support: Research reports that “a third of newly organized bargaining units still do not have a first contract after three years” [SES 3]. Writing about Canada, one source says: “Other research has found that first-contract arbitration helped more Canadian workers sign first contracts.” [UNN 25]

HR5408_C07.support: A U.S. Treasury review reports: “Unions raise the wages of their members by 10 to 15 percent.” [UNC 3] The review says close-election studies “only measure the effect of election wins, but not of successful contracts” [SEP 6], and that “This leads to an underestimate of the effect of a first union contract on outcomes.” [SEP 6] The panel must consider “the employees' cost of living” [UNC 1].
HR5408_C07.response: A close-election study covering 1984–2001 reports that “estimates for wages are close to zero” [SES 19] and that “unions have been somewhat unsuccessful at securing significant wage gains.” [SES 19] Treasury also reports “evidence that the wage premium is smaller for recent union hires” [SEP 6]. The study does not estimate first-contract arbitration, and Treasury’s point about elections without contracts is not answered by it.

HR5408_C08.support: A Canadian study found: “FCA reduces first agreement work stoppage incidence by at least 50 percent.” [SES 4] It says Canadian labor laws are “modeled on U.S. labor law.” [SES 4] It explains the result this way: “creating an incentive for the parties to bargain in good faith and negotiate an agreement” [SES 4]. Separately, a binding decision gives the two sides an ordinary way to end a dispute without a stoppage.

HR5408_C09.support: Representative Walberg warns that contracts “could mandate spending that small employers cannot sustain” [SES 28]. Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe warns: “Panel arbitrators may not understand the business” [UNC 16].
HR5408_C09.response: The decision must be based on “the employer's financial status and prospects” [UNC 1] and “the wages and benefits other employers in the same business provide their employees.” [UNC 1] Canadian boards and arbitrators report “a very conservative approach to first contract awards” [UNC 8]. A 2009 review reports: “Experienced arbitrators generally believe that interest arbitration rarely results in a departure from the status quo in terms of economic and noneconomic working conditions.” [SES 14] The status quo is the existing situation. This evidence describes practice elsewhere, so it does not show that such an award could never occur.

HR5408_C10.support: The Heritage Foundation, a policy research group, states: “Currently, nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” [UNC 2] The bill says “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute” [UNC 1]. The bill does not provide for a member vote on that decision.

HR5408_C11.support: One group warns of “work and safety rules that are not adequately tailored to a facility's specific operations” [UNC 20]. Another warns that “outside arbitration panels unfamiliar with local construction markets could impose contract terms that fail to reflect the industry or local labor standards.” [UNT 19]

HR5408_C12.support: A former labor-board chair wrote that the requirement “would presumably significantly increase the demand for the FMCS’s services” [SES 5]. FMCS reports it “limited its involvement to facilities that provide health care services with bargaining units of 250 or more members, and to bargaining units of 1,000 members or more for all other industries in which it has jurisdiction.” [SES 23] Lawyers warn: “The FMCS does not have anywhere near the personnel to meet the obligations this legislation would impose upon it.” [UNC 24]

HR5408_C13.support: First-contract delay can weaken a new union: “delay frustrates workers and undermines their union.” [TR 20] SEIU includes “working people in the public and private sector” [TR 21]. It exempts a national payment for “members who have not achieved a first collective bargaining agreement.” [TR 21] It sets money aside for “political education and political action purposes” [TR 21]. AFT says “$2.90 of each member’s per capita tax shall be set aside each month in a special fund” [TR 22] supporting “political activities” [TR 22]. It represents “more than 75,000 educators in charter schools who are considered private sector employees.” [TR 23] The AFL-CIO requires payment “upon the full paid-up membership of each affiliated national or international union” [TR 28].

ui_copy.strengthGuide: Compare the overall case for each direction. Look at the different consequences in the accepted arguments. Consider all of the effects, not only the strongest one. Do not count headings. If two arguments describe the same consequence, count it once. Good evidence for an effect does not mean that the effect is large. There is no formula to calculate a winner. Choose Pending if you have no justified comparison.
ui_copy.mappingGuide: Does a shared claim seem too broad for this argument? Does a supporting path seem to be missing? Explain the problem in the optional note.
